title: Why Are There So Few Cows in America Right Now?
summary: Have you noticed that hamburgers and steaks cost more lately? One big reason: there are fewer cows in the United States than at any time in the last 75 years! The U.S. had only 86.2 million cattle this year, the lowest number since 1951. Why? Farmers are dealing with a lot of problems. It's more expensive to feed and care for cows because fuel, equipment, and fertilizer cost more. Some farmers are selling their cows because prices are high right now, but they're not buying new ones because it's too risky. Droughts and wildfires, made worse by climate change, also hurt farms. Plus, many farmers are getting older—the average age is 58—and not enough young people are starting farms. Another scary threat is a bug called the New World screwworm. It lays eggs inside animals, and the babies eat them alive. It's been found in Mexico, close to the U.S. border. Even though there are fewer cows, we still have plenty of beef because cows today are much bigger than they were in the 1950s. But with high demand and low supply, prices at the grocery store will likely stay high for a while.
why_it_matters: If beef prices stay high, your family might spend more money at the grocery store, which could mean less for other things you enjoy, and it might encourage us to eat more plant-based foods or chicken.

background_read: The United States has the largest beef industry in the world, and cattle farming has been a big part of American history.
Climate change (the Earth getting hotter because of pollution) has caused more frequent droughts and wildfires, making farming harder.
The New World screwworm (a deadly fly that lays eggs in wounds on animals) was once eliminated in the U.S., but it has been found in Mexico recently.
Article_Structure: WHO: Farmers, ranchers, and consumers in the United States.
WHAT: The number of cows has dropped to its lowest level in 75 years, causing beef prices to rise.
WHERE: Farms across the United States, with threats like droughts and the screwworm near the Mexico border.
WHY: Because of rising costs for feed, fuel, and fertilizer, droughts and wildfires made worse by climate change, an aging farmer workforce, and the threat of a harmful bug near the border.

perspectives.description: It's getting harder to make a living because everything costs more, and climate change is causing more disasters. Some of us are selling off our herds now while prices are high, but we worry about the future.
Becoming a farmer seems too risky and expensive, with uncertain weather and huge debts, so many of us choose other careers.
We're paying much more for burgers and steak, and it might force us to eat less beef and try other foods.
